The workers sat at the field on Sundays and some residents called the police.
The residents were unwelcoming to the workers.

The residents saw the workers as a threat even when they did nothing wrong. They 'called the police though we were only eating'. Calling the police on people having a meal shows the residents were suspicious of the workers themselves, not of anything they did.

The writer's mother has dementia and the nearest centre is 40 minutes away by bus.
There is not enough care for the elderly near the estate.

Care is too far away for a family to use while holding a job. The nearest centre is '40 minutes away by bus', and the writer 'gave up my job' to mind her mother. When care is that far, the burden falls on the family.

Source A tells me that residents can vote from 1 to 14 March, online or at the booth beside the market, and that every household has one vote.
The message is that residents now have real power over how the money for the estate is spent.

The message is that residents now have real power over how the money for the estate is spent. The poster says 'This year YOU decide how $500,000 is spent' and promises 'The projects with the most votes will be built'. The capital letters and the firm promise show that the choice belongs to the residents and not to the council. It is speaking to every household in the estate. It wants them to believe that their vote counts, so that they take part.

Source E is useful. It shows that the higher price did make households save water: 'Households used 4% less water per person in the first six months'. So the rise did what it was meant to do. Source D is reliable. It says 'households used 4% less water per person' and 'That is the biggest drop in ten years'. These are clear facts and figures, so it shows that the rise was the right decision.

Source D is not fully reliable. It says 'The rise has worked' because 'households used 4% less water per person'. Source E gives the same figure, so that part is true. But E says 'the fall was uneven': large flats and houses 'cut their use by 1%' while one-room and two-room flats 'cut by 9%'. D also says rebates 'covered most of the rise', yet E found that in the smallest flats one in five now 'flush or wash less often than they think is healthy'. Source A says that the school has been in the estate for 58 years and that people should sign before 30 April.
The message is that the school is worth far more than its pupil numbers show, so it should not be closed.

The message is that the school is worth far more than its pupil numbers show, so it should not be closed. The petition says 'A school is not a shop that closes when it has fewer customers' and 'Small classes mean every teacher knows every child by name'. This shows that the writers see the small size as a strength and not as a reason to close. It is speaking to people who live in the estate. It wants them to believe that the school can still be saved, so that they sign.
